title: Caching & Delivery
summary: How to stop doing the same expensive work twice. 4 building blocks drilled by recall: the signal that says reach for one, what it costs, how it breaks, which sibling rules it out, and what it is doing across the canonical problems.
keyTakeaways: Cache — A fast store holding the answer to work you already did, so the expensive path runs once for many reads.
CDN — A globally distributed cache of your static bytes, serving users from a nearby PoP instead of your origin.
Hot-Key Mitigation — Techniques for the one key whose traffic exceeds what a single shard or cache node can serve — replicate it, split it, or absorb it locally.
Edge Compute — Running small amounts of your logic in the CDN's PoPs, so personalisation, auth or rewriting happens near the user instead of at origin.

questions.prompt: A design prompt says: The prompt gives a lopsided read:write ratio — 100:1 and up; The answer is expensive to compute or fetch and changes far more slowly than it is read. Which building block answers that, and why is it the right reach?
points: Cache — A fast store holding the answer to work you already did, so the expensive path runs once for many reads.
The prompt gives a lopsided read:write ratio — 100:1 and up
The answer is expensive to compute or fetch and changes far more slowly than it is read
A stated staleness tolerance ('feed can be up to a minute old') is an explicit invitation
questions.answer: Cache. A fast store holding the answer to work you already did, so the expensive path runs once for many reads. You reach for it when: The prompt gives a lopsided read:write ratio — 100:1 and up; The answer is expensive to compute or fetch and changes far more slowly than it is read; A stated staleness tolerance ('feed can be up to a minute old') is an explicit invitation.

questions.prompt: You put Cache in a design. Name the signals that should have stopped you — and what it costs even when it is the right call.
points: Reads must reflect writes immediately — a cache is a correctness hazard you added on purpose
The working set is uniformly random over a huge keyspace; the hit rate will not pay for the machinery
Write-heavy workloads where you would spend more invalidating than serving
Every cache is a second copy of the truth, and now you own the invalidation problem
Memory is expensive, so capacity forces an eviction policy you must justify
Debugging gets harder: behaviour now depends on whether something was warm
questions.answer: Don't reach for it when: Reads must reflect writes immediately — a cache is a correctness hazard you added on purpose; The working set is uniformly random over a huge keyspace; the hit rate will not pay for the machinery; Write-heavy workloads where you would spend more invalidating than serving. And it is never free: Every cache is a second copy of the truth, and now you own the invalidation problem; Memory is expensive, so capacity forces an eviction policy you must justify; Debugging gets harder: behaviour now depends on whether something was warm.

questions.prompt: Cache is in your design and load goes up ten times. How does it break?
points: Stampede — a hot key expires and every concurrent request hits the origin at once
Hot key — a single entry exceeds one node's throughput no matter how many nodes you add
Cold start after a flush or deploy sends full production load at a database sized for cache-miss traffic
Silent staleness: an invalidation is missed and wrong data is served indefinitely with no error
questions.answer: Stampede — a hot key expires and every concurrent request hits the origin at once Hot key — a single entry exceeds one node's throughput no matter how many nodes you add Cold start after a flush or deploy sends full production load at a database sized for cache-miss traffic Silent staleness: an invalidation is missed and wrong data is served indefinitely with no error

questions.prompt: Cache vs CDN vs Inverted Index / Search — what decides between them?
points: CDN — Same idea moved to the network edge. Pick a CDN when the payload is static and the win is geographic distance.
Inverted Index / Search — If reads are QUERIES rather than key lookups, a precomputed index beats caching every distinct query.
Cache — A fast store holding the answer to work you already did, so the expensive path runs once for many reads.
questions.answer: CDN: Same idea moved to the network edge. Pick a CDN when the payload is static and the win is geographic distance. Inverted Index / Search: If reads are QUERIES rather than key lookups, a precomputed index beats caching every distinct query.

questions.prompt: Cache appears in 13 of the canonical design problems. Name as many as you can, and say what it is doing in each.
points: Design a URL Shortener — Hot short-code → long-URL lookups. The mapping is immutable once created, so there is no invalidation story to get wrong — only capacity and TTL.
Design a News Feed — The per-user timeline of post IDs in Redis, hydrated to full post bodies on read. The cache IS the precomputed feed, not an optimisation over it.
Design a Distributed Rate Limiter — The counter state itself. Limiter state is small, extremely hot, and worthless once stale — which is exactly the shape an in-memory store is for.
Design a Leaderboard — Top-N slices per leaderboard window, so the overwhelmingly common 'show me the top 100' read never touches the underlying ranking structure.
Design a Distributed Cache — The whole problem. Ring placement, replication and eviction all exist to make one cache survive nodes joining and leaving without losing its value.
Design a Typeahead / Autocomplete Service — Precomputed top-K completions per prefix, held in memory because the keystroke budget is tens of milliseconds and a rebuild is a batch job.

Design a Ticket Booking System (Ticketmaster-style) — Event and seat-map reads, which vastly outnumber bookings. Availability counts are cached loosely on purpose; the actual hold stays transactional.
Design an LLM Inference Platform — Prompt-prefix and KV-cache reuse across requests, so a shared system prompt is not recomputed per call — the dominant saving in LLM serving.
Design a RAG / Semantic Search System — Embeddings and retrieval results for repeated queries, since embedding a query costs a model call every single time.
Design a Proximity Service — Popular geo cells, whose query volume is wildly skewed toward a few dense urban areas. A short TTL absorbs most reads before the index sees them.
Design a Feature Store — The online store is a cache by another name: precomputed features in a low-latency store, because inference cannot wait for a batch job to finish.
Design an Authentication & Session Service — Session and token-validation state, so every authenticated request is not a database read. Revocation is what makes the TTL choice genuinely hard.

Design a Sanctions Screening System — Adjudications are cached rather than raw matches, so a name a human already cleared against the current list version does not re-enter the review queue on every payment.

The mapping is immutable once created, so there is no invalidation story to get wrong — only capacity and TTL. in Design a News Feed, the per-user timeline of post IDs in Redis, hydrated to full post bodies on read. questions.prompt: A design prompt says: The payload is large, static and read by many people — images, video segments, JS bundles; The prompt names a global user base and latency is a stated requirement. Which building block answers that, and why is it the right reach?
points: CDN — A globally distributed cache of your static bytes, serving users from a nearby PoP instead of your origin.
The payload is large, static and read by many people — images, video segments, JS bundles
The prompt names a global user base and latency is a stated requirement
Origin egress bandwidth is the thing that will not scale
questions.answer: CDN. A globally distributed cache of your static bytes, serving users from a nearby PoP instead of your origin. You reach for it when: The payload is large, static and read by many people — images, video segments, JS bundles; The prompt names a global user base and latency is a stated requirement; Origin egress bandwidth is the thing that will not scale.

questions.prompt: You put CDN in a design. Name the signals that should have stopped you — and what it costs even when it is the right call.
points: Responses are personalised per user — you are caching a thing with an audience of one
Content must be revoked instantly; purge propagation is not immediate
The bottleneck is compute, not distance or bandwidth
You now have cache state in hundreds of places you cannot inspect
Purge is eventually consistent and often billed per request
Cache-key design becomes a real engineering problem the moment headers or query strings vary
questions.answer: Don't reach for it when: Responses are personalised per user — you are caching a thing with an audience of one; Content must be revoked instantly; purge propagation is not immediate; The bottleneck is compute, not distance or bandwidth. And it is never free: You now have cache state in hundreds of places you cannot inspect; Purge is eventually consistent and often billed per request; Cache-key design becomes a real engineering problem the moment headers or query strings vary.

questions.prompt: CDN is in your design and load goes up ten times. How does it break?
points: Stale asset served long after deploy because the URL did not change
Cache fragmentation: a varying header splits one hot object into thousands of cold ones
Origin shielding absent, so a cold global cache means every PoP independently stampedes the origin
questions.answer: Stale asset served long after deploy because the URL did not change Cache fragmentation: a varying header splits one hot object into thousands of cold ones Origin shielding absent, so a cold global cache means every PoP independently stampedes the origin

questions.prompt: CDN vs Cache vs Edge Compute — what decides between them?
points: Cache — An origin-side cache when the win is compute, not distance.
Edge Compute — When the response must be assembled per request but you still want it done near the user.
CDN — A globally distributed cache of your static bytes, serving users from a nearby PoP instead of your origin.
questions.answer: Cache: An origin-side cache when the win is compute, not distance. Edge Compute: When the response must be assembled per request but you still want it done near the user.

questions.prompt: CDN appears in 4 of the canonical design problems. Name as many as you can, and say what it is doing in each.
points: Design a Photo-Sharing Service — Serves the image bytes themselves, so origin egress does not scale with viewer count and users fetch from a nearby PoP.
Design a Video Streaming Service — Distributes video segments — the economics of the whole design, since origin bandwidth for video is the cost that dominates everything else.
Design a Live Streaming Service — Delivers HLS/DASH segments to viewers, which is what makes a million-concurrent-viewer broadcast affordable at all.
Design a Short-Form Video Feed — Prefetches and serves the next videos in the feed, because perceived instant playback is the product's core interaction.
questions.answer: CDN carries different work in each: in Design a Photo-Sharing Service, serves the image bytes themselves, so origin egress does not scale with viewer count and users fetch from a nearby PoP. in Design a Video Streaming Service, distributes video segments — the economics of the whole design, since origin bandwidth for video is the cost that dominates everything else. in Design a Live Streaming Service, delivers HLS/DASH segments to viewers, which is what makes a million-concurrent-viewer broadcast affordable at all. in Design a Short-Form Video Feed, prefetches and serves the next videos in the feed, because perceived instant playback is the product's core interaction.

questions.answer: Hot-Key Mitigation. Techniques for the one key whose traffic exceeds what a single shard or cache node can serve — replicate it, split it, or absorb it locally. You reach for it when: The prompt contains a celebrity, a viral item, or a flash sale on one SKU; Load is skewed enough that adding shards does not help because the skew rides along; One partition is saturated while the rest of the fleet is idle.

questions.prompt: You put Hot-Key Mitigation in a design. Name the signals that should have stopped you — and what it costs even when it is the right call.
points: Load is genuinely uniform; you are solving a problem the workload does not have
The hot entity needs strong consistency — replicating it multiplies the write-coordination cost
Key splitting (key#1..key#N) pushes fan-in complexity to every reader
Local in-process caches multiply staleness windows by the number of app servers
Detection needs per-key telemetry you probably are not collecting yet
questions.answer: Don't reach for it when: Load is genuinely uniform; you are solving a problem the workload does not have; The hot entity needs strong consistency — replicating it multiplies the write-coordination cost. And it is never free: Key splitting (key#1..key#N) pushes fan-in complexity to every reader; Local in-process caches multiply staleness windows by the number of app servers; Detection needs per-key telemetry you probably are not collecting yet.

questions.prompt: Hot-Key Mitigation is in your design and load goes up ten times. How does it break?
points: Mitigation applied statically, so yesterday's celebrity is replicated and today's is melting a shard
Split counters read before all sub-keys are summed, producing numbers that go backwards
The hot key is a WRITE key, so replication makes contention worse rather than better

questions.prompt: Hot-Key Mitigation vs Consistent Hashing vs Cache — what decides between them?
points: Consistent Hashing — Solves uneven placement, not uneven demand. Virtual nodes will not save you from one viral key.
Cache — A local cache tier in front absorbs read skew without touching the sharding scheme.
Hot-Key Mitigation — Techniques for the one key whose traffic exceeds what a single shard or cache node can serve — replicate it, split it, or absorb it locally.
questions.answer: Consistent Hashing: Solves uneven placement, not uneven demand. Virtual nodes will not save you from one viral key. Cache: A local cache tier in front absorbs read skew without touching the sharding scheme.

questions.prompt: Hot-Key Mitigation appears in 4 of the canonical design problems. Name as many as you can, and say what it is doing in each.
points: Design a News Feed — The celebrity account: one write with tens of millions of followers, which is precisely the case that breaks naive fan-out-on-write.
Design a Leaderboard — One popular leaderboard absorbs most of the reads and writes, so its sorted set has to be split or replicated away from the others.
Design an Ad Click Aggregator — A viral campaign concentrates click events on a single aggregation key, saturating whichever partition happens to own it.
Design a Proximity Service — Dense urban cells hold vastly more entities and receive vastly more queries than the rest of the grid, by orders of magnitude.

questions.prompt: You put Edge Compute in a design. Name the signals that should have stopped you — and what it costs even when it is the right call.
points: The logic needs your primary database — you have moved the compute but not the data
Anything requiring long execution, large memory, or strong consistency

questions.prompt: Edge Compute is in your design and load goes up ten times. How does it break?
points: Edge logic diverges from origin logic and the two disagree about the same request
A bad edge deploy has global blast radius and no gradual rollout
Cold starts add latency to exactly the requests you moved to the edge to speed up

questions.prompt: Edge Compute vs CDN vs API Gateway — what decides between them?
points: CDN — If the variation can be pushed into the URL, plain CDN caching is simpler and faster.
API Gateway — Central policy at origin when consistency of the rule matters more than the round trip.
Edge Compute — Running small amounts of your logic in the CDN's PoPs, so personalisation, auth or rewriting happens near the user instead of at origin.
questions.answer: CDN: If the variation can be pushed into the URL, plain CDN caching is simpler and faster. API Gateway: Central policy at origin when consistency of the rule matters more than the round trip.
